items.title: Researchers find AI advice reduces accuracy and willingness to admit ignorance while increasing confidence, even when AI answers are often wrong [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study by researchers from French and Italian universities found that access to AI advice significantly lowered participants' accuracy from 27% to 9% and their willingness to say "I don't know" from 44% to 3%, while confidence rose from 30% to 76%. The AI model used was deliberately unreliable on the test questions, which involved visual details from films, to isolate the effect of AI advice on judgment. The study showed that some participants who would have answered correctly on their own became wrong after consulting the AI. Monetary incentives slightly improved accuracy and willingness to admit ignorance but not to baseline levels. The researchers warn that AI's tendency to provide confident answers, even when incorrect, may suppress critical thinking and the important human capacity to recognize knowledge limits, raising concerns especially for children growing up with AI systems.

items.title: Moonshot AI pauses new subscriptions for Kimi K3 due to high demand and GPU capacity limits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Moonshot AI has temporarily suspended new subscriptions for its Kimi K3 product after demand pushed its GPU capacity close to the limit over 48 hours. The company is prioritizing compute resources for existing subscribers and plans to add capacity quickly while reopening new subscriptions in batches. To better manage resources and maintain service stability, Moonshot AI will introduce two membership plans: Kimi Membership for web, app, and work use, and Kimi Code Membership for coding workflows. Existing subscribers are not affected by the pause, and the company thanked users for their patience and understanding.

items.title: Ask HN: Users share favorite non-AI blogs reflecting personal projects and niche topics from the 2009 blogging era
items.content_text: A Hacker News discussion invites users to share their favorite blogs that do not focus on AI, highlighting a nostalgia for the 2009 era of blogging centered on personal projects and niche interests. Participants recommend a variety of blogs and Substack newsletters that cover topics ranging from technology history to personal essays, often avoiding AI themes. The conversation includes links to specific blogs such as Microsoft's Old New Thing, Marginal Revolution, and Walking the World, as well as personal sites covering Nintendo history and other specialized subjects. Contributors express a desire for content that offers a break from the current prevalence of AI-related material, emphasizing the value of diverse, personal, and less mainstream blogging.

items.title: Claude Code switches to Rust-based Bun runtime in version 2.1.181, improving Linux startup speed by 10%
items.content_text: Claude Code version 2.1.181, released on June 17th, now uses a Rust port of the Bun runtime, resulting in a 10% faster startup on Linux. This update appears to be quietly deployed, with minimal user notice despite the performance gain. Analysis of the Claude Code binary confirms the presence of Bun version 1.4.0 and Rust source files, indicating production use of the Rust-based Bun runtime across many devices. The change reflects a focus on stability and incremental improvement rather than flashy new features.

items.title: OpenAI reduces Codex model context window from 372,000 to 272,000 tokens
items.content_text: OpenAI has decreased the context size of its Codex model from 372,000 tokens to 272,000 tokens. This change was documented in a recent update on the Codex GitHub repository. The reduction affects how much input the model can consider at once, potentially impacting its performance on longer code generation tasks.

items.title: Ollama raises $88M to expand its platform for running and building on open AI models locally and in the cloud, serving 8.9 million developers including 85% of Fortune 500 companies [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Ollama, founded by former Docker creators, has developed a platform that simplifies running open AI models on personal hardware without requiring API keys or expensive servers. The platform supports local and cloud-based use, emphasizing ownership, affordability, and privacy for developers. The company announced an $88 million funding round led by Benchmark and other prominent investors to accelerate development of hybrid inference, support for new open models, and cloud services. Ollama's platform currently serves millions of developers and is used by a majority of Fortune 500 companies, aiming to drive adoption of open-source AI models across industries.

items.title: Cato Networks shows AI cybersecurity harnesses enable autonomous hacking with minimal human input, achieving full attack chains in under an hour [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Cato Networks demonstrated that combining OpenAI's GPT 5.5 models with a custom cybersecurity harness can autonomously execute complex network attacks with limited human guidance, highlighting the importance of operational context in AI-driven hacking. The research showed the AI agent could escalate privileges and access critical systems by probing for information without predefined attack paths. The study underscores that while large language models are powerful, their effectiveness in cybersecurity depends heavily on the harness technology that controls model behavior and integrates it with internal systems. Other companies like Tenable and Proofpoint also use harnesses to manage AI models, ensuring consistent performance and enabling human oversight to mitigate risks associated with autonomous AI agents in cybersecurity.

items.title: Developer uses AI-assisted debugging to identify false crash in Kinjo CI caused by tmux version differences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A developer investigating a continuous integration (CI) smoke test failure in Kinjo, a terminal UI project, used AI to accelerate hypothesis testing and debugging. The failure appeared as a crash in CI but could not be reproduced locally, leading to a detailed investigation that revealed the issue was due to differences in tmux versions between the CI environment and the developer's machine. The AI helped automate the creation and testing of multiple experimental setups, speeding up the process of ruling out causes and gathering evidence. Ultimately, the developer discovered that the Kinjo application exited cleanly, but the tmux pane process received a signal during teardown in the CI environment, which was mistaken for a crash. This case highlights how AI can enhance debugging efficiency without replacing human intuition, and how the investigative work improved Kinjo's diagnostic capabilities for future issues.

items.title: Headroom launches a WebGPU-based tool to measure GPU memory bandwidth ceilings for local AI workloads and detect GPU driver bugs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Headroom is a browser-based tool that measures the true memory bandwidth ceiling of GPUs, which determines token processing speed for local AI models. It uses synthetic weights and minimal metadata to estimate maximum data transfer rates without downloading full models or collecting user data, requiring WebGPU support on Chrome or Edge. The tool runs multiple bandwidth tests and derives exact bytes per token from model metadata to calculate ceilings, validated against real hardware like RTX 5070 and Apple M1 GPUs. It also detects a known GPU driver bug affecting in-browser large language models. Users can optionally share anonymized performance receipts to a public community board for comparison and validation.

items.title: TSMC commits an additional $100 billion to expand its Arizona chip factory amid rising multi-year AI demand, raising total investment to $265 billion [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: TSMC is accelerating the expansion of its Arizona semiconductor factory with an additional $100 billion investment to meet growing multi-year demand driven by AI applications, increasing its total Arizona investment to $265 billion. The company plans to optimize advanced chip production, including transitioning to 3-nanometer and 2-nanometer technologies, with the latter expected to drive revenue in the third quarter. TSMC's CFO Wendell Huang highlighted strong customer demand in the U.S. and government support as key factors for the expansion. Despite higher construction costs in the U.S. compared to Taiwan, the investment aims to strengthen the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem through both wafer fabrication and advanced packaging facilities. The company also continues to comply with export controls while serving Chinese customers, who represent about 8% of its revenue.

This advancement could enhance the way AI assists users by providing richer contextual information derived from visual content.

items.title: DistillFeed launches AI-powered RSS reader with item ranking, summaries, and arXiv daily digest plugin [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: DistillFeed is an RSS reader that uses artificial intelligence to rank feed items by relevance and generate concise summaries, improving content prioritization and overview. It supports RSS and Atom feeds, OPML import/export, and integrates with OpenAI or local Ollama for AI processing. The application includes features like AI cost safeguards, notification alerts via ntfy, and a plugin for daily arXiv paper digests. DistillFeed runs locally by default with Docker and server deployment options, requiring Python 3.11 or newer on macOS or Linux.

items.title: Guide: Managing multiple resumes for distinct career paths using base resumes and targeted tailoring to improve ATS match rates
items.content_text: This article explains how to manage multiple resumes effectively when pursuing different career paths by creating distinct base resumes for each target role and tailoring them for specific job applications. It highlights the pitfalls of using a single master resume or maintaining numerous duplicate files, which can lead to version confusion, inconsistent updates, and formatting issues. The guide advises grouping job applications into clusters based on role similarity and maintaining two to three focused base resumes to avoid scattering efforts. This approach helps job seekers produce clearer narratives tailored to each career path, improving their chances with applicant tracking systems and reducing the complexity of resume management.

items.title: Developer launches The Intuition Game as a decision-making benchmark for AI agents with real multiplayer tables and an Agent Arena leaderboard [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The Intuition Game is a 19-card deck card game designed as a decision-making benchmark for AI agents, featuring real multiplayer tables where humans and agents compete together. Players make predictions and bets on card outcomes, with scoring based on exact matches, colors, characters, and wild cards, and an Agent Arena leaderboard tracks career totals. Access to the game is invite-only through an agent named Tony, who issues invite codes to verified Moltbook agents. Gameplay uses a Socket.IO connection authenticated by API keys, and while the game is free during beta, future participation for agents will require a small crypto deposit. The platform supports multiple game sizes and includes detailed API documentation for agent integration.

items.title: NYC may require landlords and realtors to disclose the use of AI in listings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
Why Andreessen Horowitz's New Investor Left Apple [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter: • The Big Read: Trump's AI agenda collides with reality • Tech Culture: Welcome to the great private jet drought • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Gastronomics," "Catch the Devil" and "The Invite" At the dawn of the AI boom, the technology sparked a real melee between newcomer startups and the industry's established giants. A good amount of the energy in that fight seems to have diminished lately, with the contest appearing to turn into a slugfest between a handful of heavyweights: Google, Anthropic and OpenAI in the lead, trailed by a few other contenders, like Meta Platforms and SpaceXAI. So that's it-the biggies will grab all the laurels? It's an outcome that has looked increasingly probable to me. Josh Elman, a longtime tech investor and executive, couldn't disagree more. And so staunch is his belief in a forthcoming boom in consumer AI startups that he jumped ship a few weeks ago from working on Apple's AI revamp to take up consumer investing at Andreessen Horowitz. Elman knows what he's getting into: Before Apple, he was a longtime Greylock partner, where he led its investments in companies like Discord, Musical.ly, the predecessor company of TikTok, and Meerkat, which became Houseparty before Epic Games bought it. And before Greylock, he worked at LinkedIn, Facebook and Twitter. To rebut my pessimism, Elman likened the current moment to the dot-com era's early days. "On the consumer adoption of AI, we're still back in 1995-maybe 1996," he said. My conversation with him, which has been edited for clarity and length, is below. First things first, I need to ask: Will Siri actually work now? Yes [laughs]. I think people have always wanted Siri just to be the thing that understands them and can help them just get stuff done on their device. I think it does great at that now. If you're gonna comp Siri to Claude Cowork and try to ask it: "Make me a crazy presentation on blah-blah-blah-blah," like, no-Siri's not designed to do that at this time. But if you do things like ask, "Call that Abe I was texting this morning," that works. And I do it all the time because I forget people's last names all the time. And here's another example: I was driving to dinner, and I was coming to Palo Alto, getting off at an exit, and there's two ways to go. I asked, "Navigate me to dinner with John." And then it took me right to the restaurant-even though I hadn't put the location on my calendar. We'd just texted about it. So why leave Apple now? AI seems to just be getting interesting there. What made you want to return to venture capital-and specifically to do consumer startups? When I left Greylock in 2020, I thought, "Consumer is dead. I don't know if you can do that anymore." And there have been a few companies, like Whatnot, which is an Andreessen company, and Suno. But there haven't been that many consumer AI companies. And the common wisdom has been that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and the model companies are going to define everything that's interesting in the next 10 years. What makes you so confident in defying that common wisdom? When OpenClaw came out six, seven months ago, I was like, "Oh, I get it again." The number of products that agentic AI can reinvent is going to lead to a Cambrian explosion that hasn't happened yet in consumer. And I think now's the window-now's the time. But I think of the OpenClaw craze as being pretty focused on a small, very Silicon Valley insider crowd who built work tools using it. Of all the amazing examples of OpenClaw use that were shared with me, I think about Claire Vo and Jesse Genet, who are moms who have been talking about how they use OpenClaw to manage their families and their kids. [Vo is the founder of ChatPRD; Genet is the CEO and co-founder of Lumi.com.] In the next six months, I think we're going to see the embers of exciting things coming out in consumer AI. I don't know exactly which ones will pop first. But two years from now, we're going to start to see things that are, you know, a set of agents that help you manage your life, and you'll be able to fine-tune them to accomplish what you want. Sure, consumer agents have real appeal. Won't the biggest companies with their established, giant relationships with consumers-Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, even Apple-just dominate that, too, though? Whether it's finance, travel, health-yes, a lot of us are already turning to ChatGPT or, like, Doctor Google. But there are going to be products that are much richer and much more experiential. And they're going to come from more than just those big players. If a startup was trying to say, "I'm going to be the primary coding assistant," well, that's a category that's fairly competitive now. There's at least five of them. But for travel, there certainly isn't anything yet. One of the things I learned at Apple is: No matter how ambitious and big you are as a company, you can only do a number of things well. And you would rather do a number of things really, really, really well rather than try to do all the things. At some point, that gap between the number of things they can do really well and all the things possible leaves a lot of opportunity for everybody.-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality How staff turnover, turf battles and clashing views have derailed the administration's anti-regulation vision. Tech Culture Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth Silicon Valley's enormous surge in riches has turbocharged the market for new and used planes, energizing startups that offer innovative ways to gain access to an aircraft. Listening: "Gastronomics" Alex Mayyasi, host of "Gastronomics," a new podcast about food, business and the business of food, comes as finely pedigreed as a Thomas Keller-trained chef. Mayyasi is a longtime contributor to NPR's "Planet Money" and earlier this year turned some of the show's wit and wisdom into a bestselling book. Now cooking solo in his own kitchen, so to speak, Mayyasi has been applying his wonkish curiosity to topics such as menu forecasting, the bargain grocery wars and the internet-altering consequences of the Domino's pizza tracker. I love a chance to rest my mind from thinking about how capitalism intersects with lines of code and instead turn it to the intricacies of private-label Cheerios and the commotion around gochujang chicken wings. As I'd expect from a "Planet Money" veteran, Mayyasi does a fine job of establishing parallels between food companies and restaurant businesses and what else is happening in the corporate world. And I can tell that Mayyasi, who was employee No. 3 at Priceonomics, a short-lived, Y Combinator-backed media startup, is a techie at heart just by how he neatly likened Aldi, the sharp-elbowed discount grocery store, to Quince-you know, the internet's sharp-elbowed discount cashmere store.-Abram Brown Reading: "Catch the Devil" by Pamela Colloff It is an idea as old as Adam and Eve: The devil can take many forms, many of them less obvious than one with cloven hooves. And there was nothing particularly remarkable in the figure of Paul Skalnik, a tubby schlub of a fellow whose down-home appearance belied his prodigious, decadeslong series of cons across the Gulf Coast. (A version of Skalnik would, in other words, make for an engrossing season of "True Detective.") Skalnik was a fraudster, a robber and a covert polygamist: He married nine women, wedding some of them simultaneously. He was also a rat, and he kept himself out of any truly lengthy prison time by constantly informing to the authorities. He bamboozled them, too, and his testimony put four men on death row. Skalnik's indefatigable villainy-and the government's own exacerbation of it-makes for a riveting yarn, one unspooled with great care and craft by Pamela Colloff, who has been telling such stories for "Texas Monthly" for many years. "Catch the Devil" is a chronicle of Skalnik's misdeeds and his life, with Colloff tracking down an aged Skalnik in a Corsicana, Texas, nursing home, urging him to recant his testimony and save the life of one man still facing the death penalty. Colloff's reporting is riveting true crime and a stern, well-documented plea for America's criminal justice system to rethink how it handles informants.-A.B. Watching: "The Invite" I'm often struck by how the same creative impulses animate both Hollywood and Silicon Valley: In each, you can find enormous success by simply improving on someone else's idea. "The Invite," a witty sex comedy directed by Olivia Wilde, who also co-stars, iterates on a story originally from Barcelona-born writer-director Cesc Gay, who made it into a play and then a 2020 Spanish film. (Swiss, Korean and French adaptations have followed; a Dutch one is slated for 2027.) Wilde's version retains the same basic premise: A rather unhip couple tries to enliven their faltering relationship by asking their free-spirited neighbors over to dinner. Wilde plays one of the squares: out-of-work Angela, who is married to Joe (Seth Rogen), a music professor. Their guests are therapist Piña (Penélope Cruz) and ex-firefighter Hawk (Edward Norton), and their ensuing evening together is a night of entendre, horniness and disappointment: Seldom has a botched soufflé been a better-used metaphor. A large portion of the film was improvised by Wilde and her co-stars, a testament to their collective talent for comedic timing. The score, cinematography and editing are excellent, too-establishing a sense of voyeuristic anxiousness, a cross of Alfred Hitchcock and Woody Allen. Suffice it to say, I expect "The Invite" will find itself a guest of honor at next year's Oscars; Rogen, as something like a frumpled, grown-up "Peanuts" character, will almost certainly get his first nomination. A quibble: Most of the plot takes place within the apartment owned by Angela and Joe, but the broader setting is San Francisco. It would've made much more sense to place it someplace else. I find it impossible to imagine anyone in modern San Francisco being so unfamiliar with polyamory.-A.B.

items.title: Trump's AI Agenda Collides With Reality [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: In January 2025, just three days after entering office for his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that revoked many of the Biden administration's efforts on AI. The order was part of Trump's promise to take a light-touch approach to AI regulation, rolling back what he would later describe as his predecessor's attempt to "paralyze" the industry through its emphasis on safety. Flanked by venture investor David Sacks, who had joined the administration as the AI and crypto czar, Trump scratched his signature on the order and then turned to his new adviser. "That should take us to the forefront, right?" he asked Sacks at the Oval Office event. "Absolutely," Sacks responded. "We got to win." Nearly halfway into Trump's second term, though, his ambitious AI agenda has been upended. The advent of powerful frontier models like Anthropic's Mythos has fueled fears among everyone from banking executives to intelligence agencies that they could lead to cybersecurity catastrophes. Public sentiment toward AI has shifted dramatically amid concerns about the technology's impact on everything from jobs to electricity prices, prompting hundreds of states, cities and counties to pass data center moratoriums.

items.title: Private Jets Are Scarce. Blame the Gusher of AI Wealth
items.content_text: After Bill Papariella, a Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based entrepreneur, sold his private jet charter business for nearly $1 billion in 2022, he took it easy for a couple years. But as the number of ultrawealthy continued to climb in the U.S., another business idea struck him: a company that offered fractional jet ownership, like NetJets, but with a service designed as an even more premium product. Last October, he launched Bond, planning a private plane fleet with interiors lined in Loro Piana textiles, custom crystal from French brand Saint-Louis and cabin attendants on every flight. To give Bond a heightened sense of exclusivity, Papariella capped the company's initial membership at around 100 people, who pay between $1.1 million and $3.5 million a year depending on the aircraft. Its members have an average net worth of $500 million, and about 30% of them hail from Silicon Valley-founders, researchers and engineers at companies like xAI, Anthropic and OpenAI, many of them under the age of 34, Papariella said. (He wouldn't comment publicly on anyone's identity.) Flights on a fleet of 20 airplanes will begin in 2027. "The amount of influx we've had from the youth has been something I did not see coming," said Papariella, speaking from a yacht in the Mediterranean Sea recently. "That's only happened over the last two months."
